passage:
Dear Professor Menon,

I hope this finds you well. I am writing to ask whether I might submit my literature assignment on Friday instead of Wednesday, as I have been unwell and behind on reading. I have attached what I have finished so far, and I will send the remainder as soon as I can. I understand if this is not possible, and I am grateful for your time.

With thanks and regards,
Uma

P.S. to Jaya (separate text): hey! sent the prof a mail asking for extension, wish me luck 🙂 will tell you what he says!! 🤞

Uma reread the two versions once more and thought about how her words changed when the reader changed.

qa.q: On which day did Uma ask to submit her assignment?
qa.a: She asked to submit it on Friday instead of Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Uma feel as she writes to the professor and then to Jaya?
qa.a: She is nervous and hopeful, asking Jaya to wish her luck, and she is polite and careful with the professor but relaxed with her friend.

qa.q: What could Uma do if she wanted the email to sound even more appropriate?
qa.a: She could keep it short, state clearly what she needs and by when, and leave out chatty phrases from her messages to friends.

qa.q: How might Professor Menon see the email?
qa.a: The professor may see it as respectful and clear, and likely to be taken seriously, though the decision still depends on the course rules.

grounding: Uma shifts between formal and informal register for a professor and a friend.

passage: I'm Lokesh, and I want to tell you about the worst email I ever sent. I was applying for a summer job at a print shop, and I'd typed it the way I text my friends: "hi, i saw the ad, want to join, when do i start?" No greeting, no name, nothing. My friend Baljeet read it over my shoulder and burst out laughing. "You wouldn't say that to an interviewer in person," he said. He wasn't unkind, and I got the point. I rewrote it: "Dear Ms. Kaur, I am writing to apply for the position advertised... I have attached my CV." It felt stiff, but they invited me for an interview the next day. I still keep the first draft as a reminder of how small choices change the impression.

qa.q: What kind of job was Lokesh applying for?
qa.a: Lokesh was applying for a summer job at a print shop.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when Baljeet laughed, and what did Lokesh take from it?
qa.a: Lokesh probably felt a bit embarrassed, but took the point that the message sounded too casual, and Baljeet's tone was not unkind.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that worked?
qa.a: Lokesh rewrote the email with a greeting, a name, a clear purpose and an attached CV, and it led to an interview.

qa.q: How might the print shop owner have seen the first draft?
qa.a: The owner might have read it as careless or unaware of norms, though Lokesh could still have been serious, and the tone left that unclear.

grounding: Lokesh learns that a person's register should match the relationship after an overly casual job email.

passage: I'm Mehak, and I was in the library with Kashish when she wrote to Professor Rao about her missed deadline. She typed: "hey sir, cant submit today, can u extend pls? thx." I leaned over and read it. "You're sending that to Rao sir?" Kashish shrugged. "It's short. He's busy." I said nothing, but I could picture Rao sir's eyebrows. She hesitated, then deleted it. She wrote again, slowly: "Dear Professor Rao, I'm writing to ask whether I might submit my assignment on Friday instead of today. My grandmother was admitted to hospital last night. I'm sorry for the inconvenience and will send it by Friday noon. Thank you for considering this. Regards, Kashish Arora, 2nd year B.Com." Then she texted her friend Priya: "grandma in hospital 😔 sir might kill me lol." Same afternoon, two completely different voices. Rao sir replied in an hour: "Of course. Hope she recovers soon."

qa.q: When did Kashish ask to submit the assignment instead?
qa.a: On Friday instead of today.

qa.q: What might Kashish have been feeling as she rewrote the email?
qa.a: She seemed hesitant and worried about how the professor would react, especially with her grandmother in hospital.

qa.q: What did Kashish change in the second email, and why did it work?
qa.a: She used a formal greeting, full sentences, a reason, an apology, a clear date and a sign-off, which showed respect and got a quick, kind reply.

qa.q: How might Professor Rao have read the first draft?
qa.a: He might have found it too casual and disrespectful, with "hey sir" and "pls", and been less willing to help.

grounding: Shows a young adult adjusting the register of an email from casual to formal for a professor, while keeping an informal voice with a friend.

passage:
Monday. Pooja got a job interview invitation and replied: "Hi!! Thanks so much, sounds awesome, see u Thurs 😊". Her flatmate Jahnavi read it over her shoulder and winced. "Pooja, that's a bank."
Tuesday. Pooja rewrote her reply to the bank's HR: "Dear Ms Sharma, thank you for the invitation. I confirm my availability for the interview on Thursday, 14 March, at 11 a.m. Please let me know if I should bring any documents. Kind regards, Pooja Nair." Jahnavi nodded. "Better." Then Pooja texted Jahnavi: "ok I sound like a robot 😅".
Friday. After the interview, the HR manager emailed: "Thank you for a clear interview. We'd like to invite you to the second round." Pooja replied in the same formal tone. Then she sent Jahnavi a voice note, screaming. "SECOND ROUND! Chai's on me!"

qa.q: When was Pooja's interview?
qa.a: Thursday, 14 March, at 11 a.m.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when she texted "I sound like a robot"?
qa.a: She felt a bit awkward and self-conscious about the formal tone, even though she knew it fit the bank.

qa.q: What did Pooja do well in adjusting her messages?
qa.a: She used a formal greeting, full details and a courteous sign-off for the bank, and kept her casual, excited voice for Jahnavi.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi see Pooja's first reply?
qa.a: Jahnavi winced, seeing that the casual tone and emoji didn't suit a message to a bank.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to adjust register between an employer and a friend to signal respect and understanding of norms.

passage: Binita, since you're writing to your first boss, let your Arnab mama tell you about my first letter to mine. I was twenty-one and had just joined a tea estate office in Jorhat. I needed two days' leave for my sister's wedding. I wrote to the manager, Mr Barua, the way I'd write to my college friends: "Barua da, need 2 days off next week, sister's wedding. Hope OK. Arnab." He called me in and held up the note. "Da? Hope OK?" My ears went red. He wasn't angry, just firm. "Here we write: 'Respected Sir, I request leave for two days, the 10th and 11th, for my sister's wedding. I will complete the accounts before I go.' You see? Same message. But now I know you respect the office." I rewrote it at his table. He signed it and even sent a gift for the wedding. I still write that way to seniors.

qa.q: Why did young Arnab need two days' leave?
qa.a: For his sister's wedding.

qa.q: How did young Arnab feel when Mr Barua held up the note?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his ears going red, realising his casual note didn't suit the office.

qa.q: What turning point in the story taught Arnab about register?
qa.a: Mr Barua firmly showed him how to write the same request formally, and Arnab rewrote it at his table.

qa.q: How did Mr Barua see the casual note?
qa.a: He saw it as too informal for the office, though he wasn't angry, and wanted Arnab to show respect in writing.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to adjust written register to a senior, with greeting, courtesy and detail that signal respect.

passage: Vijay had twelve minutes before the hostel Wi-Fi shut off at midnight, and two messages to send. The first was to Ujjwal: "bro can u bring my charger to lab tmrw, dying here 😩". Easy. The second was to Professor Rao, asking for an extension on the thermodynamics assignment because his grandmother was in hospital. His thumbs, still in chat mode, typed: "hi sir can i get 2 more days for assgnmt, family thing." He stared at it. That was how he'd talk to Ujjwal, not to someone grading his work. With nine minutes left, he deleted it and started again: "Dear Professor Rao, I am writing to request a two-day extension for Assignment 3. My grandmother was admitted to hospital on Monday, and I have been with her. I will submit by Friday. Thank you for considering this. Regards, Vijay Kumar, Roll No. 42." He sent it with a minute to spare. At eight the next morning the reply came: "Granted. I hope she recovers soon."

qa.q: By which day did Vijay promise to submit?
qa.a: By Friday.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when he stared at the first draft?
qa.a: He felt uneasy that the chatty tone would seem careless or disrespectful to someone grading his work.

qa.q: What made the second email suit its reader?
qa.a: A formal greeting, a clear request with the reason, a firm new deadline, thanks, and his full name and roll number.

qa.q: How might Professor Rao have read the first draft if it had been sent?
qa.a: As rushed and casual, which could have made the request seem less serious.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult adjusting register between a text to a friend and an email to a professor, using greeting, courtesy and length to fit the relationship.
